guidance: A planning model, not an edit: it assumes the speed changes in a straight line across the whole clip and that the retime is applied before any other trim, transition or render setting.
method: Playback speed is expressed as a multiple of normal speed, and the ramp holds it on a straight line from the first source frame to the last: with a start speed s1, an end speed s2 and a source length T seconds, the speed at source time t is s1 + (s2 - s1) t / T. A source frame lasts 1 / s seconds of output at constant speed, so the output length is the integral of 1 / s(t) from 0 to T, which is T x ln(s2 / s1) / (s2 - s1) when the two speeds differ and T / s1 when they are equal. A five second clip at a constant 50 percent becomes ten seconds and at 200 percent becomes two and a half, as the editing manuals state. The length is symmetric in the two speeds, so a ramp from 25 to 100 percent lasts as long as one from 100 to 25 percent over the same source; only where the slow part sits changes, which is what the checkpoints show. Because the ramp passes quickly through the fast end and lingers at the slow end, the average speed is source length divided by output length, not the mean of the two percentages: 100 to 25 percent over four seconds averages 54.1 percent, not 62.5. The output time of any source point is the same integral up to that point, so the checkpoint list answers where a beat, a cut or a title has to sit on the retimed clip. Frame counts are the length multiplied by the project frame rate and rounded to the nearest whole frame, both for the source and for the output; a frame-based retime quantises each source frame to whole output frames, so an editor's own count can differ by a frame or two, and the longest a single source frame stays on screen is 1 / slowest speed output frames. Speeds run from 5 to 400 percent, source length from 0.1 to 3,600 seconds, and the frame rate must be one of 23.976, 24, 25, 29.97, 30, 50, 59.94 or 60. Reverse speeds, multi-segment ramps, speed transitions, pitch handling, frame interpolation and render quality settings are not modelled. Everything is calculated in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Apple, Create variable speed effects in Final Cut Pro: a variable speed effect changes playback speed dynamically and a ramp is a gradual transition between two speed segments
